articles.title: This Tourette’s wrist device cut tics by a quarter in a UK trial
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM In a 2023 clinical trial of 121 people in the UK, wearing a prototype wrist device reduced tic frequency by an average of 25 percent. The Tourette’s wrist device, called Neupulse, came out of research at the University of Nottingham, and three years on, the people using it describe […]
The post This Tourette’s wrist device cut tics by a quarter in a UK trial first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

In a 2023 clinical trial of 121 people in the UK, wearing a prototype wrist device reduced tic frequency by an average of 25 percent. The Tourette’s wrist device, called Neupulse, came out of research at the University of Nottingham, and three years on, the people using it describe its effect in far stronger terms than a one-in-four reduction would suggest.

How a Tourette’s wrist device targets tics

Rhythmic pulses to the median nerve

Neupulse sends rhythmic electrical pulses into the median nerve, which runs through the wrist and into the hand. Trials have shown that this stimulation changes activity in the brain regions responsible for movement control, and that the rhythm of the pulses can lower both the frequency and the intensity of tics. The device was developed by the university and its spin-out company, Neurotherapeutics Ltd, which secured £1 million (about $1.3 million) in additional funding to bring it to market.

Stephen Jackson, the Nottingham professor who has led the research, described the response from users as “a dream come true.” Some of the feedback he has received is very concrete. “We’ve had people saying they managed to get through their wedding vows without ticking,” he said. Others told the team they could move through an airport and board a flight without tics.

Tourette’s syndrome in the UK

Tourette’s syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition, usually beginning in childhood, that causes involuntary sounds and movements known as tics. More than 300,000 people in the UK have it, according to the charity Tourettes Action, and there is no cure. The condition reached a wider audience in 2023 when singer Lewis Capaldi, who has Tourette’s, tried the device before a concert in Nottingham, and again through the film I Swear, a drama based on the life of Tourette’s campaigner John Davidson.

Three users, three measurable changes

Katie, 15: years of constant vocal tics

Katie, from Hertfordshire, started having tics at age seven. Her snorting tic ran almost nonstop, to the point of leaving her with a sore throat that kept her in bed for two weeks, and it disrupted her sleep, her eating, and her school attendance. “It was constantly moving, constantly making sounds and then I was kind of getting looked at like, ‘why are you doing that?'” she said. Her mom, Julia, called it “heartbreaking” to watch. “You feel helpless. You feel you don’t know where to turn really,” she said.

After reading about the Nottingham research, Julia brought Katie to try the device in December, before it went on sale. The effect was immediate, Katie said, and she became “really calm.” “It was absolutely life-changing. It was like the best day of my life,” she said. On the drive back to Hertfordshire, she “just cried the whole way home.”

Ollie, 15: a different diagnosis, a similar response

Ollie’s case extends the picture, because he does not have Tourette’s. Nearly two years ago he cracked his neck, and about 48 hours later the movement had become involuntary and constant. “It was incredibly sudden,” he said. He was later diagnosed with functional neurological disorder (FND), a condition that affects how the brain sends and receives signals. His father, Alex, said sleeping, eating and drinking all became “incredibly difficult.” Ollie stayed inside for about a month at one stage and missed six to seven months of school ahead of his GCSEs, the exams British students sit around age 16.

He came close to telling his parents not to bother with the device. A few months ago, when he switched it on for the first time, he phoned home. “You could hear that he was crying on the telephone because it had worked and his neck movement had stopped,” Alex said. Ollie put it this way: “It’s like a light switch. I remember my hands were quite shaky when I was calling my parents because it’s like getting part of your life back.”

Mylo, 17: from trial participant to owner

Mylo, from Buckinghamshire, was 13 when he joined the 2023 trial. He recently received his own device as a gift and said the urge to suppress his facial tics went away “instantaneously.” “As soon as it comes on, I can feel it,” he said. “I feel different… I feel new almost, which is strange.”

Why Neupulse is not yet an NHS treatment

Wellness product versus medical device

The device comes in two versions. Neupulse-C is sold as a consumer wellness product, and the university says “thousands” have been purchased. Neupulse-M is the version intended for marketing as a medical treatment for tics and Tourette’s syndrome, and it is still working through regulatory approval. That distinction determines whether the National Health Service can offer it.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has identified the technology as “promising” but asked for more evidence of long-term benefit. In 2025, it said its committee would meet again to assess the device’s clinical and cost-effectiveness. “They were unable to recommend it for use in the NHS until we have the regulatory approval,” Jackson said. “That’s something we’re working towards.” He hopes to see the Tourette’s wrist device available through the NHS “in the next year or so.”

Early reports from the Tourette’s community

Emma McNally, CEO of Tourettes Action, said the users she has spoken with have given the device “nothing but praise.” “Some people have said it’s helped them to go to places that they’ve not been for a long time, such as the cinema or a library,” she said. Others told her it helped them come out of a tic attack and feel more relaxed.

Wrist stimulation beyond Tourette’s syndrome

The Nottingham team is now testing the same approach on other conditions. Early trials have examined whether the pulses can reduce tremors in people with Parkinson’s, and Jackson said the university plans a UK-wide clinical trial covering anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The next milestone is regulatory, since medical approval for Neupulse-M would open the door to NICE guidance and NHS prescriptions, and the trials that follow will show whether a signal sent through the wrist can shape movement and mood in conditions well beyond tics.

articles.personality_title: UK trial shows wrist device cuts Tourette’s tics by 25%
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Tourette’s syndrome is a condition that causes people to make involuntary movements or sounds called tics. In the UK, over 300,000 people live with Tourette’s, but there is no cure. Researchers at the University of Nottingham have been working on a wrist device called Neupulse to help reduce these tics.

**What happened** – In 2023, a clinical trial with 121 participants tested a prototype of Neupulse. The device sends gentle electrical pulses to the median nerve in the wrist, which affects brain areas controlling movement. Wearing the device lowered the number of tics by about 25 percent. Users reported feeling calmer and able to do things that were previously hard, like speaking without tics or moving through busy places.

**Impact** – This device offers a real, measurable way to improve life for people with Tourette’s. For example, a 15-year-old girl named Katie said it was “life-changing” because it stopped her constant vocal tics. **What’s next step** – The Neupulse-M version is being reviewed by health regulators and may become available through the UK’s National Health Service (NHS) in the next year or so. Researchers are also testing if similar wrist stimulation can help other conditions like Parkinson’s disease, anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new wrist device from UK research has been shown to reduce Tourette’s tics by a quarter, offering hope for better daily life and new treatments ahead.

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.summary: A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
articles.content:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.

Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity

The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."

What the Eight-Year Study Revealed

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant, well-documented scientific study revealing that certain types of screen time can positively impact children's cognitive development, challenging common negative assumptions. It provides detailed findings from an eight-year longitudinal study with broad implications for child development, education, and parenting, emphasizing balanced, active, and mentally stimulating screen use alongside physical activity. This has meaningful societal relevance as it informs healthier approaches to children's screen use and physical activity, potentially improving cognitive outcomes for many children.
articles.personality_title: Finnish study finds some screen time linked to better teen thinking skills
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people believe screen time harms children's brain development, but a long study in Finland aimed to see how screen use and physical activity affect thinking skills as kids grow up.

**What happened** – Over eight years, researchers followed 260 Finnish children, tracking their screen time, physical activity, and brain abilities. They used both questionnaires and wearable devices to measure movement and heart rate. The study found that kids who spent more time on screens tended to have better cognitive processing as teenagers. They also discovered that the type of activity mattered: using screens for learning or problem-solving was more helpful than just watching videos. Physical activity affected boys and girls differently, with girls benefiting from light exercise and boys from guided sports.

**Impact** – This study challenges the common idea that all screen time is bad. It shows that what children do on screens can help their thinking skills. Also, it highlights that different kinds of physical activity support brain health in different ways for boys and girls. These details can help parents, teachers, and doctors guide children to use screens and exercise in ways that support learning and memory.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to do more studies where they change kids’ activities on purpose to see what causes improvements in brain skills. They also want to understand better how exercise intensity and screen activities affect brain development over time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using screens for learning and problem-solving, combined with the right kind of physical activity, may help children's thinking skills as they grow into teenagers.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une étude finlandaise montre que certains temps d'écran améliorent les capacités de réflexion des adolescents
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup pensent que le temps d'écran nuit au développement cérébral des enfants, mais une longue étude en Finlande a cherché à comprendre comment l'utilisation des écrans et l'activité physique influencent les capacités de réflexion des enfants.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Pendant huit ans, des chercheurs ont suivi 260 enfants finlandais, mesurant leur temps d'écran, leur activité physique et leurs capacités mentales. Ils ont utilisé des questionnaires et des appareils portables pour mesurer les mouvements et le rythme cardiaque. L'étude a montré que les enfants passant plus de temps devant les écrans avaient de meilleures capacités de traitement cognitif à l'adolescence. Ils ont aussi découvert que le type d'activité comptait : utiliser les écrans pour apprendre ou résoudre des problèmes était plus bénéfique que de simplement regarder des vidéos. L'activité physique avait des effets différents selon le sexe, les filles bénéficiant d'exercices légers et les garçons de sports encadrés.

**Impact** – Cette étude remet en question l'idée que tout temps d'écran est mauvais. Elle montre que ce que les enfants font sur les écrans peut améliorer leurs capacités de réflexion. Elle souligne aussi que différents types d'activité physique soutiennent la santé cérébrale différemment chez les filles et les garçons. Ces informations peuvent aider parents, enseignants et médecins à mieux orienter les enfants vers des usages d'écran et d'exercice favorisant l'apprentissage et la mémoire.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent réaliser d'autres études où ils modifient volontairement les activités des enfants pour voir ce qui améliore leurs capacités cérébrales. Ils veulent aussi mieux comprendre comment l'intensité de l'exercice et les activités sur écran influencent le développement du cerveau à long terme.

**Une phrase clé** – Utiliser les écrans pour apprendre et résoudre des problèmes, combiné au bon type d'activité physique, peut aider les capacités de réflexion des enfants en grandissant.
articles.personality_title_es: Estudio finlandés revela que cierto tiempo frente a pantallas mejora habilidades de pensamiento en adolescentes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas creen que el tiempo frente a pantallas daña el desarrollo cerebral de los niños, pero un estudio largo en Finlandia buscó entender cómo el uso de pantallas y la actividad física afectan las habilidades de pensamiento a medida que los niños crecen.

**Qué pasó** – Durante ocho años, investigadores siguieron a 260 niños finlandeses, midiendo su tiempo frente a pantallas, actividad física y habilidades mentales. Usaron cuestionarios y dispositivos portátiles para medir movimiento y ritmo cardíaco. El estudio encontró que los niños que pasaban más tiempo en pantallas tendían a tener mejor procesamiento cognitivo en la adolescencia. También descubrieron que el tipo de actividad era importante: usar pantallas para aprender o resolver problemas era más beneficioso que solo ver videos. La actividad física afectó de forma diferente a niños y niñas, con las niñas beneficiándose de ejercicios suaves y los niños de deportes guiados.

**Impacto** – Este estudio desafía la idea común de que todo el tiempo frente a pantallas es malo. Muestra que lo que los niños hacen en las pantallas puede ayudar a sus habilidades de pensamiento. Además, destaca que diferentes tipos de actividad física apoyan la salud cerebral de distintas maneras en niños y niñas. Esta información puede ayudar a padres, maestros y médicos a guiar mejor a los niños hacia usos de pantallas y ejercicios que apoyen el aprendizaje y la memoria.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren hacer más estudios donde cambien las actividades de los niños para ver qué causa mejoras en las habilidades cerebrales. También quieren entender mejor cómo la intensidad del ejercicio y las actividades en pantalla afectan el desarrollo cerebral con el tiempo.

articles.title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.
articles.content:
A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open new possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.

The findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.

Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.

Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms

The discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.

Worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling important features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.

To investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.

The researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.

"We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12."

Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.

These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.

Although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.

The discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.

"Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases," says Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery where vitamin B12 reversed developmental abnormalities in a model organism with a mutation linked to a rare genetic disorder, Verheij syndrome. This finding has broad implications for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic diseases, offering hope for new therapies beyond the studied syndrome. The research is well-contextualized, with evidence from both model organisms and human patient data, indicating a meaningful positive impact on health and medical science.

**What happened** – Scientists studied tiny worms with a gene mutation similar to one found in Verheij syndrome patients. These worms grew slowly and stayed smaller than normal. Researchers discovered that this mutation affected how the worms used vitamin B12 in their metabolism. When the worms were given extra vitamin B12, their growth problems were mostly fixed.

**Impact** – This is important because it shows vitamin B12 can directly improve problems caused by a genetic mutation related to a rare disease. The same vitamin B12-related changes were also found in human patients with Verheij syndrome. This suggests vitamin B12 might lead to new treatments for this and possibly other genetic disorders involving similar cell processes.

**What's next step** – Scientists will need to test whether vitamin B12 supplements can help people with Verheij syndrome in real life. Further research will explore how vitamin B12 affects metabolism in these diseases and if it can be used as a therapy.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Researchers found that vitamin B12 can reverse developmental problems in worms with a gene mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, pointing to new treatment possibilities for this rare disorder.

articles.title: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with surprising hotspots of inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about cardiac aging and could help researchers develop new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.
articles.content:
As the heart gets older, inflammation increases, but scientists have not fully understood where these changes occur or which parts of the organ are most affected. Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) have now uncovered a surprising pattern: Certain regions of the heart appear to be hotspots for aging-related inflammation, offering new clues about how the heart changes over time.

In a study of mouse hearts published in Aging Cell, the researchers discovered that signs of inflammation and tissue scarring were especially concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root. These areas contain immune cells and connective tissue cells whose interactions change with age, potentially affecting the surrounding heart muscle. The findings provide a new picture of cardiac aging and could guide future efforts to understand cardiovascular disease.

"Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue," said study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX. "We really have to think of aging as something that is not linear, because just like we know that people don't age at the same rate, what we know now is that organs and tissues don't age at the same rate either, even within one individual."

Much of the previous research on heart aging has centered on cardiac muscle, particularly the left ventricle. This chamber performs the essential task of pumping blood into the aorta and throughout the body. By studying the heart as a whole, rather than concentrating primarily on its muscle, the JAX team uncovered important changes in other tissues and the ways their cells interact.

"The valves and the major blood vessels are parts often thought of as plumbing rather than the main engine, but this is a very complicated little machine," Rosenthal said. "It turns out they're home to many of the cells we're interested in, and that's where some of the most important aging-related signals were concentrated."

Mapping Hidden Hotspots of Heart Aging

Growing older is the single greatest risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet many of the cellular processes responsible for the heart's decline remain poorly understood. One challenge is that mammalian heart muscle cells have very little ability to regenerate or replace themselves. To investigate what happens as the heart ages, Rosenthal and her colleagues used advanced techniques that allowed them to study thousands of individual cells from young and old mice while also identifying their locations within the heart.

Scientists already know that aging is accompanied by a persistent, low level of inflammation throughout the body. Earlier studies have found similar changes in the heart, including an increase in immune cells that regulate inflammatory activity (macrophages) and cells that produce and maintain connective tissue and contribute to scar formation (fibroblasts).

The new analysis showed that aging macrophages became more active in genes involved in inflammation and changes to tissue structure. Fibroblasts, meanwhile, increasingly displayed molecular characteristics associated with fibrosis (or scarring). Crucially, the researchers went beyond identifying which genes were active. They also mapped the locations of these cells, making it possible to see how different regions of the heart change as they grow older.

This approach revealed that inflammation and fibrosis (or scarring) were not distributed uniformly. Instead, the strongest signals appeared around the heart valves and aortic root. The researchers believe these regions may act as important centers of cardiac aging, where changes in supporting cells could influence the health of nearby heart muscle.

"To keep muscle cells happy, the other cells in the heart have to continue supporting them throughout life," Rosenthal said. "What this study does, for the first time, is provide a comprehensive picture of how those support cells, particularly fibroblasts and macrophages, change with age and contribute to what we call inflammaging."

Surprising Signs of Aging in Young Hearts

Another unexpected discovery challenged assumptions about how scientists identify aging cells. The team examined molecular markers frequently associated with cellular senescence, a state in which cells permanently lose the ability to divide, often because of aging or stress. As senescent cells accumulate, they can contribute to ongoing inflammation, tissue damage, and diseases associated with older age.

Surprisingly, some of these supposedly age-related markers were already present in young mouse hearts. Their presence suggests that the markers alone cannot reliably establish whether a cell has entered senescence, and that their meaning may depend on where they appear and the condition of the surrounding tissue.

"What surprised us was that some of these markers that have been associated with aging were already present in young hearts. They weren't where anyone expected to find them, and that forced us to rethink what those markers are telling us," Rosenthal said. "That turns the usual interpretation of cardiac aging on its ear because these markers alone don't mean a cell is senescent. There's nothing senescent about a six-month-old mouse heart."

The researchers also identified genes that became more active with age and were especially prominent in the same regions. Among them were Ccl8, which helps transmit inflammatory signals, and Cdkn1a (also known as p21), a gene widely used as an indicator of cellular senescence. Their locations provided further evidence that the valves and aortic root may be particularly important areas for understanding how the heart ages.

"We're not talking about single genes. We're talking about an entire conversation between immune cells and fibroblasts. As the heart ages, the way those cells communicate changes, and that shift appears to be linked to the inflammation and tissue remodeling we see in older hearts," Rosenthal said.

Male and Female Hearts Show Different Aging Patterns

The study uncovered another important distinction: Aging did not produce exactly the same molecular changes in male and female mouse hearts.

In males, aging fibroblasts showed stronger connections to biological processes associated with fibrosis. In females, the corresponding changes were more closely related to pathways involved in heart development and protein production.

Rosenthal noted that these differences may offer clues about cardiovascular aging in humans. Heart disease tends to become more common in women after menopause, while its development in men generally follows a more gradual pattern. The distinct cellular changes observed in male and female mice could help researchers investigate the biological processes behind these differences.

However, the results describe differences in molecular activity, not demonstrated differences in heart function or disease risk. Further research will be needed to determine how these patterns influence cardiovascular health.

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the team compared the mouse results with previously published data from human hearts. Several molecular processes associated with aging, including pathways involved in responding to cellular stress, appeared in both species. This overlap suggests that at least some of the biological changes identified in mice may also be relevant to human heart aging.

"Our findings change the focus from aging across the entire heart to specific anatomical hotspots, helping us better understand how inflammation and fibrosis are connected and which regions of the heart are involved in the aging process," said study author Amalia Sintou, a postdoctoral associate at JAX.

Could These Discoveries Help Protect Aging Hearts?

Although the research does not yet identify a new treatment, it offers scientists a more detailed understanding of where aging-related changes occur and which cells are involved. By revealing these cellular patterns, the findings could help guide future studies aimed at reducing cardiovascular decline, maintaining healthy heart function, and improving health later in life.

Rosenthal's team is now examining whether exercise, diet, and disease alter the interactions between immune cells and connective tissue cells. The researchers hope to distinguish the normal effects of aging from changes that may leave the heart increasingly vulnerable to cardiovascular problems.

The experimental design also helped the team isolate aging itself as a contributing factor. Because the mice lived under the same conditions and received the same diet, the researchers could investigate age-related changes without the additional variation introduced by different environments or eating habits.

"Valve replacement is common in older adults, and one of the big questions is how much of the underlying damage is driven by aging itself," said study author Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, a postdoctoral associate at JAX. "Because all of the mice in our study lived in the same environment and ate the same diet, we were able to isolate the effects of aging and show that aging alone can initiate some of these changes in the valves and aorta."

Together, the findings suggest that understanding heart aging requires looking beyond the muscle responsible for pumping blood. The valves, major blood vessels, and supporting cells may play a much larger role than previously recognized. Learning how these structures change and communicate over time could eventually help scientists identify ways to preserve cardiovascular health as people age.

Research Funding and Study Authors

The research received funding from the NIH Common Fund through The Jackson Laboratory Senescence Tissue Mapping Center (JAX-Sen TMC U54 AG079753). Additional support came from JAX's National Cancer Institute-designated Cancer Center (P30 CA034196).

Additional authors from The Jackson Laboratory included Yue Zhao, Antonios Somarakis, Harshpreet Chandok, Juliana Alcoforado Diniz, Ramalakshmi Ramasamy, Gretchen T. Clark, Brian S. White, Paul Robson, Ron Korstanje, and J. Matthew Mahoney. Leon Frommer and Sikander Hayat of RWTH Aachen University also contributed to the study.

**Context** – Scientists have long studied how the heart ages, usually focusing on the heart muscle. Aging often leads to inflammation and scarring, but it was unclear which parts of the heart were most affected.

**What happened** – Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory studied hearts from young and old mice. They also discovered that some signs of aging appeared even in young hearts. The study showed that different cells, like immune cells and connective tissue cells, change and communicate differently as the heart ages.

**Impact** – This discovery changes how scientists understand heart aging. **What's next step** – The research team plans to study how lifestyle factors like exercise and diet affect these aging processes. They hope this will help separate normal aging from harmful changes, leading to better ways to protect the heart as people grow older.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Heart aging happens unevenly, with valves and blood vessels showing the most inflammation and scarring, offering new clues to protect the heart over time.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques découvrent que le cœur vieillit de manière inégale avec des points chauds d'inflammation
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques ont longtemps étudié le vieillissement du cœur, en se concentrant généralement sur le muscle cardiaque. Le vieillissement entraîne souvent une inflammation et des cicatrices, mais il n'était pas clair quelles parties du cœur étaient les plus touchées.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs du Jackson Laboratory ont étudié les cœurs de souris jeunes et âgées. Ils ont découvert que l'inflammation et les cicatrices étaient particulièrement fortes autour des valves cardiaques et des gros vaisseaux sanguins, et non principalement dans le muscle cardiaque comme on le pensait auparavant. Ils ont également constaté que certains signes de vieillissement apparaissaient même dans les cœurs jeunes. L'étude a montré que différentes cellules, comme les cellules immunitaires et les cellules du tissu conjonctif, changent et communiquent différemment avec l'âge.

**Impact** – Cette découverte change la compréhension du vieillissement cardiaque. En identifiant des points chauds spécifiques où le vieillissement est le plus actif, la recherche ouvre de nouvelles pistes pour préserver la santé du cœur. Elle a aussi révélé des différences dans le vieillissement des cœurs mâles et femelles, ce qui pourrait expliquer pourquoi les maladies cardiaques évoluent différemment chez les hommes et les femmes.

**Prochaine étape** – L'équipe de recherche prévoit d'étudier comment les facteurs liés au mode de vie, comme l'exercice et l'alimentation, influencent ces processus de vieillissement. articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren que el corazón envejece de forma desigual con puntos clave de inflamación
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han estudiado durante mucho tiempo cómo envejece el corazón, enfocándose generalmente en el músculo cardíaco. El envejecimiento suele causar inflamación y cicatrices, pero no estaba claro qué partes del corazón se veían más afectadas.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores del Jackson Laboratory estudiaron corazones de ratones jóvenes y viejos. Descubrieron que la inflamación y las cicatrices eran más fuertes alrededor de las válvulas cardíacas y los grandes vasos sanguíneos, no principalmente en el músculo del corazón como se pensaba antes. También encontraron que algunas señales de envejecimiento ya estaban presentes en corazones jóvenes. El estudio mostró que diferentes células, como las inmunitarias y las del tejido conectivo, cambian y se comunican de manera diferente con la edad.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo cambia la forma en que se entiende el envejecimiento del corazón. Al identificar puntos clave donde el envejecimiento es más activo, la investigación señala nuevos lugares para enfocar esfuerzos en mantener el corazón saludable. También reveló diferencias en cómo envejecen los corazones de machos y hembras, lo que podría ayudar a explicar por qué las enfermedades cardíacas se desarrollan de forma distinta en hombres y mujeres.

**Próximo paso** – El equipo planea estudiar cómo factores del estilo de vida, como el ejercicio y la dieta, afectan estos procesos de envejecimiento. Esperan así distinguir mejor el envejecimiento normal de los cambios dañinos, para proteger mejor el corazón con el tiempo.

**Mensaje en una frase** – El envejecimiento del corazón ocurre de forma desigual, con las válvulas y vasos sanguíneos mostrando más inflamación y cicatrices, lo que ofrece nuevas pistas para proteger el corazón con el paso del tiempo.
